extracted.intended_audience: journalism educators and university administrators planning teaching facilities (newsroom, graphics lab, radio/film) at small-to-midsize institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for designing, equipping, and budgeting newsrooms and graphics laboratories so they meet program needs immediately while allowing future expansion; targeted at smaller colleges/universities. Includes layout suggestions, equipment choices tied to industry practice, and sample budgets/diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan around individual program requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important considerations in the planning of physical facilities are the individual program requirements of the institution in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess your institution's program size (majors, projected growth), courses required (newswriting, editing, graphic design, advertising copywriting), and whether disciplines (journalism, broadcasting, speech) will be combined. Tailor space, equipment, and capacity to those specific curricular needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for immediate use with capacity for future growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide facilities for immediate use with the capacity for future growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make installations usable quickly (the paper aimed for readiness in four months) while wiring, furniture, and layout should allow addition of more expensive technology later (e.g., video display terminals, OCR, photo typesetter, ATMS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size newsroom to appropriate student capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Space for 12 students provides an ideal number for teaching newswriting and will sustain the number of students anticipated for the next two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for current cohort sizes but leave room for modest expansion (e.g., add five more typing stations by moving equipment). Include an editing desk for reporters plus an editor's slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-use newsroom design (print and broadcast)
rubrics_metrics.description: The newsroom was designed to be used for both the print and broadcast programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan shared spaces and equipment that can serve multiple program functions while considering scheduling and noise/conflict issues. Make layout and wiring flexible to support different media (typewriters, terminals, film editing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select equipment aligned with current industry standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose equipment used by major newspapers (e.g., IBM Selectric II) because industry practice affects graduates' employability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey local/regional employers to select hardware students will encounter on the job (for instance, IBM Selectric units for OCR-prepared copy); favor compatibility with university systems (IBM 370) if economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize durable equipment over economy models
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience at other institutions had shown that it did not pay to use 'economy' models of equipment which did not stand up to the rugged use of students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in reliable, commercial-grade machines rather than cheaper consumer versions; this reduces downtime and replacement costs in student labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide sufficient electrical wiring and HVAC
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional electrical wiring to provide for future equipment expansion cost $500. It was also necessary to provide air conditioning to make the facilities usable year-round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for extra wiring (110V circuits and capacity for future higher-power equipment) and air conditioning from the start; older buildings may require costly retrofits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include film editing capability but plan relocation if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Film editing capability was included but later removed to free space; removing film editing equipment allowed additional typing stations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If space is constrained, plan temporary placement for film editing with the option to move it later. Consider how moving equipment affects capacity and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design desks and furniture for functionality and future tech
rubrics_metrics.description: An editing desk was designed for five reporters plus the editor's slot. This unit is wired for the addition of three video display terminals which will connect with the university's IBM 370.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom desks should include wiring conduits, adequate surface area, and modularity to accept future video terminals, printers, or other tech. Consider typing surfaces, chair ergonomics, and storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach relevant technologies—focus on cold-type paste-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Since virtually all newspapers have now adopted the cold-type paste-up system of operation, no consideration was given to teaching the actual mechanics of letterpress preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align teaching tools and exercises with industry-standard production methods (e.g., paste-up systems) rather than obsolete technologies; this informs equipment and consumables needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate graphics lab workspace and layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 12 students can use the work area comfortably; when the radio studio is moved the capacity will be 15. There are two 46" x 32" light tables, two 46" x 32" paste-up tables, and a 12' flat work table built over the low storage cabinets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify table sizes, number of light tables, paste-up tables, and flat work surfaces to match class sizes; include storage cabinets and seating to support sustained hands-on work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include essential graphics equipment (stripprinter, hot wax, trimmer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The adding of a hot wax machine and a paper trimmer make this a small, but self-sufficient graphics facility. A Stripprinter chosen because type fonts cost only $6.00 so a great variety of type can be made available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchase core graphics devices (stripprinter and processor, fonts, waxer, trimmer) to allow students to set headlines and produce mock-ups economically; choose models suited to rooms without plumbing if necessary (simple processing unit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for operating supplies in budgeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the addition of operating supplies (including tape machines, scissors, border tapes, etc.) which might normally be included in a yearly operating budget, the original graphics lab budget fell $150 short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recurring consumables and smaller tools in initial budgeting to avoid shortfalls; list miscellaneous operating supplies explicitly and estimate costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate equipment vs. physical work costs in budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Budgets were broken out into equipment/supplies and physical work (carpet/ceiling installation, electrical wiring, air conditioning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare line-item budgets separating hardware, supplies, and construction/installation costs so hidden retrofit expenses (wiring, HVAC, carpeting) are visible and funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for shared-space scheduling conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: The graphics laboratory temporarily shared facilities with a radio studio. The only real problem that this presented was one of space. Careful scheduling prevents most conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple programs share rooms (graphics, radio, film), create schedules and usage policies to minimize conflicts; anticipate peak lab times and coordinate curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make economic choices by leveraging institutional resources
rubrics_metrics.description: While the IBM system is not the ideal choice for a newsroom, it does make economic sense since the university has an operating IBM 370.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose technology compatible with campus-wide systems to reduce cost and leverage existing compute resources; sometimes compromise on 'ideal' equipment to gain interoperability and savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide modest, realistic plans for smaller institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: While these plans might have limited use at a major university which measures students by the hundred rather than by the score, they are workable and economical for smaller institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale facilities to realistic enrollment figures and budgets of small colleges; focus on core capabilities and expand as resources permit rather than overbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate future automated/text management systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Late in 1974 or early in 1975 grant money should be available for an IBM Advanced Text Management System (ATMS/DOS/VS) which will utilize the three video display terminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan wiring, desk space, and terminal locations with anticipation of future text management and automated typesetting systems so upgrades can be integrated with minimal disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surveys of local media to inform equipment choices
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey of newspapers in southern Indiana showed that new reporters were being paid a bonus if they were familiar with preparation of copy on the IBM's for scanning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform local industry surveys to determine which skills and equipment familiarity will give students an employment advantage; let employer expectations drive key purchases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sample equipment lists and costs for planning
rubrics_metrics.description: The document provides detailed equipment lists and costs for newsroom and graphics lab (e.g., 5 IBM Selectric II @ $460, light tables, stripprinter, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete example budgets and equipment lists as starting points; adapt quantities and models to your institution's size and current price levels.
